fixes.explanation: Right, baker. Paul says the married man is concerned about “…the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife…” That's what's on his mind, compared to the unmarried man. Pleasing his wife is the very thing Paul names, and the next words tell us what it does to his interests.

Yes, baker. Paul says the married man's “…interests are divided.” I think divided means his attention has more than one place to go. The verse sets that beside the unmarried man, who is concerned about the work of the Lord.

Right, baker. Paul says, “I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord.” That's his reason, in his own words. He says it's for their good, and he says it's not meant to restrict them.

Close call, but Paul does say it. The verse reads, “From now on those who have wives should live as if they had none…” He says it right after telling the brothers that the time is short. Then he keeps going with the same "as if" for weeping, joy and purchases, and verse 31 ends with the reason: this world in its present form is passing away.

Nothing in this verse says the things of this world belong to the church, friend. Paul's reason is, “For this world in its present form is passing away.” He isn't talking about who owns anything. I think he's talking about how tightly to hold on, since the world as it is now is passing.

Word and deed is a nice pair, but it isn't Paul's pair. He says she is concerned about how she can be “…holy in both body and spirit.” I think that's him naming the whole person, outside and inside, with nothing left out.

Paul does say it, friend. The verse reads, “I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord.” Both of those goals are right there in his words. And he says it's for their good, not to restrict them.

Paul doesn't say anything about a broken word here. He says, “…let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married.” Marrying her is the answer Paul gives that man, and he says plainly it isn't sin.

That's right, baker. Paul describes a man who is “…firmly established in his heart and under no constraint, with control over his will and resolve in his heart not to marry the virgin…” Of that man Paul says, “…he will do well.” That's verse 37, and all those conditions come before it.
That's right, baker. Paul closes with, “And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” He says “I think” there, and I bet that's him giving his judgment, like he said back in verse 25.

Apollos, an eloquent Jew from Alexandria (Acts 18:24), doesn't show up anywhere in this passage. Paul's last line is, “And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” Nobody's approval is mentioned there. The thing he says he thinks he has is the Spirit.
